To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there is a strong positive relationship between the degree to which a topic is perceived as taboo and the degree to which people are willing to censor speech on that topic, (2) this relationship holds across different types of speech, and (3) the relationship between perceived taboo status and willingness to censor speech is stronger among those who are more politically liberal.

The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the case of taboo topics, it is not obvious that the harms that result when scholars are censored or held to higher evidential standards are outweighed by the harms that result from the publication of findings.

, when inquiring into the societal costs and benefits of debate around taboo topics, it is crucial to distinguish between the effects of debate itself and the effects of the findings that are discussed.
, in the absence of clear evidence that stifling debate does more good than harm, we should err on the side of allowing debate to occur.
